title: Recording, mixing: Dear Friend by Wings | 1971
content:
Studio Two, EMI Studios, Abbey Road
Producer: Paul McCartney
Engineers: Tony Clark, Alan Parsons

The final recording session for Wings’ debut album Wild Life took place on 16 October 1971.

The only song still incomplete was ‘Dear Friend’, Paul McCartney’s reconciliatory gesture towards John Lennon.

Often I would think of John, and what a pity it was that we’d argued so publicly and so viciously at times. At the time of writing this song, in early 1971, he’d called the McCartney album ‘rubbish’ in Rolling Stone magazine. It was a really difficult time. I just felt sad about the breakdown in our friendship, and this song kind of came flowing out. ‘Dear friend, what’s the time?/Is this really the borderline?’ Are we splitting up? Is this ‘you go your way; I’ll go mine’?
Paul McCartney
The Lyrics: 1956 To The Present

Lennon and McCartney had spoken on the telephone two days earlier, during which Lennon proposed liquidating Apple, and their ongoing legal issues with Maclen, which had been set up to publish their songs in the US. One solution suggested by Lennon was for McCartney to sell his share of Apple to the other three former Beatles, which was rejected by McCartney.

McCartney had commissioned Richard Hewson to score ‘Dear Friend’ for eight violins, four cellos, four flutes, two French horns, two trombones, oboe, tenor saxophone, and harp. Hewson conducted the session musicians, with McCartney producing in the studio control room.

With the recording complete, a stereo mix was made by studio engineer Tony Clark. However, it led to a disagreement, with Linda McCartney suggesting that the orchestra was overpowering and should be removed altogether. With the session continuing into the following morning, Clark filled two tape reels with mixes until everyone in the band was happy.

With ‘Dear Friend’ there was quite a creative process with Paul and myself, with his ideas about how to place the orchestral sound into that track. At the beginning, it’s placed very low, and I think it’s slightly phased as well, and it gives a really sort of mysterious sound – rather then it being a full, lush orchestra. Then, it just builds towards when the sax comes in, when the brass comes in. Making it feel just slightly tense. If you’d left it as a natural balance, that wouldn’t have been the case.
Tony Clark, 16 February 2017
The McCartney Legacy: Volume 1: 1969-73, Allan Kozinn, Adrian Sinclair
